title: Design a Global Video Delivery Network
summary: Netflix-scale delivery — deciding which titles live on which edge caches, predicting demand, and failing over across CDNs when one degrades.

slides.markdown:
The prompt: serve a catalog of millions of titles to a global audience with minimal buffering, regardless of where a viewer is or which title they pick.

This isn't [design-video-streaming-platform](design-video-streaming-platform)'s question of how one video gets transcoded — it's a placement and routing problem: which edge locations hold which titles, and what happens when the nearest edge doesn't have what a viewer wants, or an entire CDN provider degrades.

**Functional:** resolve a playback request to a nearby edge holding the requested title, keep serving through a regional CDN outage, and prioritize which titles get pre-positioned where.

**Non-functional:** a startup-latency target (first byte in low hundreds of milliseconds worldwide), a rebuffer-rate ceiling, and tolerance for wildly uneven **regional demand skew** — a title trending in one country can be nearly cold in another, so a single global caching policy underserves both.

slides.sectionTitle: Back-of-envelope: catalog size vs edge capacity vs origin egress on a miss
slides.markdown:
A catalog of 5M titles at ~5GB average (a few renditions each) is ~25PB — far more than any single edge cache can hold, which is usually sized in the tens of terabytes. So each edge holds maybe 0.1-1% of the catalog at once, meaning **cache hit ratio**, not raw capacity, is the number that determines user experience.

If even 2% of requests miss every edge and fall back to origin, and origin egress cost/capacity is sized for that miss rate, a spike to 10% misses (say, from a catalog-wide event) can be an order-of-magnitude spike in origin load — origin has to be sized for the miss tail, not the average.

The core call is a **playback manifest request**: given a `videoId` and the viewer's approximate location, return chunk URLs pointed at the nearest edge that's healthy and likely to have the title cached — not always the geographically closest one if that edge is degraded or a known cold spot for this title.

This makes the manifest resolver a routing decision, not a static lookup: it needs live signals (edge health, recent cache-hit rates per title-region) to answer correctly, which is why it can't be a dumb DNS-based nearest-edge redirect alone.

slides.sectionTitle: Cache placement: which titles go to which edges
slides.markdown:
Placement policy usually blends three signals: a title's **global popularity** (top-N titles get pushed nearly everywhere), **regional popularity** (a local hit show gets pre-positioned only in its region's edges), and **recency** (new releases get provisioned ahead of their release time, since a cold-start miss storm on day one is entirely predictable).

The fallback for everything else is reactive: an edge pulls a title from a regional cache or origin on first miss and caches it locally, evicting by an LRU-like policy so cold long-tail titles don't permanently occupy edge space that hot titles need.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: origin, regional caches, edge caches, and the request path
slides.markdown:
![Three-tier cache pyramid from origin down to edge, with the play-request path](assets/cache-tier-pyramid.svg)

Each tier absorbs most of the traffic the tier above it would otherwise see: edges should satisfy the vast majority of requests, regional caches catch most of what edges miss, and origin should see only a small residual — the tiers exist specifically so origin never sees full catalog-scale traffic.

assets.alt: Three-tier cache pyramid from origin down to edge, with the play-request path

slides.sectionTitle: Predictive pre-positioning: pushing trending titles before demand hits
slides.markdown:
Waiting for organic cache misses to populate an edge works for steady-state catalog traffic, but it fails badly for predictable spikes: a new season's release, a marketing push, or a title trending after a news event. **Predictive pre-positioning** pushes that content to relevant edges *before* the spike, using known release schedules and, for open-ended trends, early-signal demand forecasting from a small set of regions.

Getting this wrong in either direction costs real money: under-predict and you eat a miss storm at origin; over-predict and you've spent edge capacity and bandwidth pushing content nobody watches.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: single-CDN vs multi-CDN with real-time routing
slides.markdown:
| | Single CDN | Multi-CDN with real-time routing |
|---|---|---|
| Failure blast radius | One provider outage takes down all delivery | Traffic shifts away from the degraded provider |
| Operational complexity | One integration, one set of dashboards | Multiple integrations, a routing layer to build and trust |
| Cost leverage | Locked into one vendor's pricing | Can shift volume to the cheaper/faster provider per region |
| Consistency of behavior | Uniform caching/latency characteristics | Behavior can differ subtly by provider, complicating debugging |

**How to decide:** at genuinely global, high-stakes scale (a service where an hour of full outage is unacceptable), multi-CDN is close to mandatory — the operational cost buys resilience that a single vendor's SLA can't fully cover.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: multi-CDN failover when one CDN degrades
slides.markdown:
![Routing layer shifting traffic from a degraded CDN A to healthy CDN B](assets/multi-cdn-failover.svg)

The routing decision has to be continuous and automatic — based on live health/error-rate/latency signals per provider per region — not a manual failover a human triggers after users have already noticed buffering.

assets.alt: Routing layer shifting traffic from a degraded CDN A to healthy CDN B

slides.sectionTitle: The bottleneck: origin overload from a cache-miss storm on an under-cached title
slides.markdown:
If a title wasn't pre-positioned and suddenly gets a burst of simultaneous requests — say a clip goes viral without warning — every edge that doesn't have it cached will miss to origin roughly simultaneously, and origin (sized for the residual, not for catalog-wide demand) can fall over.

The standard fix is **request collapsing at the regional tier**: the first miss for a title fetches from origin once and populates the regional cache, while concurrent misses for the same title wait on that one fetch instead of each independently hammering origin — turning a thundering herd into a single origin request.

slides.sectionTitle: Trade-off: cache hit ratio vs storage cost of over-provisioning every edge
slides.markdown:
Every edge could, in principle, hold the entire catalog to guarantee a 100% hit ratio — but storage at thousands of edge locations is expensive, and most of that storage would sit unused since any one location only ever sees a fraction of the catalog's demand.

**How to decide:** size each edge to the working set that region actually requests (informed by observed regional demand skew), and accept a small, well-understood residual miss rate absorbed by the regional tier — chasing a 100% edge hit ratio spends far more on storage than it saves in avoided regional-tier hops.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: routing purely by geography, ignoring health and cost
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Always route each viewer to the geographically nearest edge or CDN — proximity is the whole optimization."

**Why it's wrong:** the nearest edge might be degraded, might not have the title cached (forcing a slow regional/origin hop anyway), or might belong to a CDN currently having a bad day in that region — geography alone ignores all of that and can route viewers straight into a known-bad path.

**Correct model:** route on live health, recent cache-hit signals, and cost together, with geography as one input among several rather than the sole decision — the goal is the fastest *actually available* path, not the shortest one on a map.
